text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Government and miners leaders reach compromise in conflict over planned mining subsidy cuts. Union leader leader Hans Berger says the spectre of mass job losses driven away.
- Health insurance schemes want a rise in contributions of around 0.5 percent.

- Otto Graf Lamsdorff, parliamentary economic spokesman for junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), criticises Chancellor Helmut Kohl's 25 billion mark investment package intended to stimulate the economy, calling it "nonsensical and risky."
- Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) due to present pension reform blueprint on Friday afternoon -- broadly in line with concepts already laid out by Labour Minister Norbert Bluem.
- Parliament in favour of improved protection of children from sexual abuse. Main parties all want to increase punishment for sex crimes.
- German DAX index of 30 leading shares falls 1.9 percent to 3,349.81 points as broad profit taking sets in.
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) want reduction of wealth accumulation.
- Head of car maker Opel David Herman says Germany is not as unattractive a business location as it is often portrayed to be.
HANDELSBLATT
- Agreement over coal subsidies. Government agrees to subsidies of 70 billion up to 2005, 1.65 billion more than originally planned.
- World's biggest computer and communications trade fair Cebit opens its doors to visitors in Hanover.
- Members of health insurance schemes and their employers will have to pay higher contributions in the future.
- Ruling by finance court in Kassel over taxes on dividend stripping business endangers independent market makers.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Immediate mass lay offs avoided in mining industry, although number of miners will be halved by 2005.
- SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine says ready for new talks on tax reform, but says return to negotiating table depends on new proposals from Kohl.
- Health insurance schemes want higher contributions.
- German welfare state in a real test period for first time in its history, says president of the Federal Constitutional Court Jutta Limbach.
- German share market considerably weaker.
DIE WELT
- Agreement over coal subsidies should avoid mass job losses over the next few years.
- Berlin forcibly repatriates first Bosnian refugees.
- New date set for construction sector wage talks after no agreement reached on Thursday.
- Harsher sentences planned for sex crimes.
